summary_paragraph: A man with a history of systolic heart failure, COPD, atrial fibrillation, and alcohol dependence was admitted for chest pain, shortness of breath, and abdominal distension after missing his medications and continuing heavy alcohol use. He was treated for a COPD exacerbation with steroids, antibiotics (later discontinued), and nebulizers, and for heart failure exacerbation with diuresis, resulting in a 5-liter fluid loss and symptom resolution. His chest pain was atypical and non-ischemic, likely related to GERD or alcohol withdrawal, and was managed with a GI cocktail. He received diazepam for alcohol withdrawal symptoms and expressed motivation to enter detox, which was arranged at discharge. An echocardiogram showed reduced ejection fraction at 35% with new cavity dilation, prompting a recommendation for primary care follow-up. Chronic pain management was transitioned from hydrocodone to higher-dose gabapentin. He was discharged home with all home medications and instructions to monitor weight and seek outpatient care.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic (congestive) heart failure
